analysis.one_liner: Lets workers unionize by signing cards instead of elections, and adds first-contract arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill had 209 cosponsors—a majority of the House—but died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Employee Free Choice Act would have changed how workers form unions. Instead of waiting for a secret-ballot election run by the government, a union could be certified once a majority of workers in a workplace signed cards saying they wanted it. If the employer and the new union could not agree on a first contract after about four months, a mediator would step in, and failing that, an arbitrator would impose a binding two-year contract. It also raised penalties for employers who fire or threaten workers for union activity, adding double-damages back pay and fines up to $20,000 per violation. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to join a union. Today an employer can delay an election for months and, even if workers vote to unionize, can refuse to ever agree on a first contract with no real penalty—unions that win elections often never get a contract. This bill short-circuits both delays: a majority of signed cards certifies the union, and a neutral arbitrator can impose a first contract if bargaining stalls. Workers fired for organizing would get back pay plus double that amount in damages, and repeat violators would face fines up to $20,000 per violation. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: If a majority of employees in a workplace sign cards authorizing a union, the National Labor Relations Board must certify the union without holding an election, removing the months-long waiting period during which employers commonly campaign against organizing. [S2] [S3]

For first contracts, the bill sets a timeline: bargaining must start within 10 days, mediation is available after 90 days, and after 30 more days an arbitration board imposes a contract binding for two years. This closes the loophole where an employer simply never agrees to a first contract. [S2] [S3]

Charges that an employer fired, threatened, or coerced workers during an organizing drive would get priority investigation, with back pay plus 2 times that amount as liquidated damages and civil penalties up to $20,000 per willful or repeated violation. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially in nonunion industries. Companies could no longer require a government-run election before a union is certified, would face a binding contract imposed by an arbitrator if they stalled on a first agreement, and would pay much more when caught violating workers' organizing rights. Some of those costs could show up as higher prices or, in a company's argument, fewer new jobs. [S3]

drawbacks.text: The card-check provision replaces the secret-ballot election. Critics argue that union organizers or coworkers can pressure people to sign cards in public view, so a signed card is weaker proof of genuine, uncoerced preference than a private ballot. The bill does require the Board to set procedures for verifying card authenticity, but it does not restore a private vote. [S3]

The binding arbitration provision means a government-appointed arbitration panel can set wages, benefits, and work rules for two years even when the two sides cannot agree—which supporters see as a needed backstop and critics see as terms no one at the company actually bargained for. [S3]

The new fines and double damages apply only to employers, not unions, and could raise business costs that get passed to customers or reduce hiring, especially for companies that would have prevailed under the current election system. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades the private ballot and open-ended bargaining for speed and enforceability. Its real target is the gap between the law on paper and the law in practice: firing or threatening union supporters is illegal today, but the penalties are small and enforcement is slow, so employers routinely absorb the cost. The card-check and arbitration provisions are the controversial parts—the pressure-on-signers objection is genuine, and imposed contracts are a blunt instrument. On balance, the bill would have materially strengthened workers' ability to unionize and bargained contracts, at a real cost to employer control over the process.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and sent to a subcommittee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2005. [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California introduced the bill on November 21, 2003, with a long list of original cosponsors including House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi and whip Steny Hoyer. [S1] [S3]
It attracted 209 cosponsors in total—200 Democrats, 8 Republicans, and 1 Independent—which was a majority of the 435-member House. [S4]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced, and on January 30, 2004 was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations. [S5]

No further action was recorded: the subcommittee and full committee never reported the bill, no markup or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced card-check certification and binding first-contract arbitration are better off, along with the committee leadership that never gave the bill a hearing or a vote despite majority support in the chamber.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the original cosponsor list.

for.name: 200 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority support in the House.

for.name: 8 House Republicans and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill across party lines.

against.name: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party control of the House agenda

against.name: Business and employer associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed card-check certification and mandatory first-contract arbitration, pressuring majority-party members to keep the bill off the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic—200 of the 209 cosponsors were Democrats, with 8 Republicans and 1 Independent joining—and the committee that buried it was run by Republicans.

industries.industry: Employers and businesses in nonunion industries
industries.note: The bill removes an employer's ability to demand a government-run election, requires a first contract within months or one imposed by an arbitrator, and multiplies the cost of firing or threatening union supporters. Its interest in the bill ran directly against the workers the bill was written for.

Unions would gain members much more easily through card-check certification and would no longer face employers who stall indefinitely on a first contract. Union membership growth is the mechanism by which workers would see higher wages and representation.

industries.industry: Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service and arbitration panels
industries.note: The bill creates a mandatory mediation-then-arbitration track for every stalled first contract, giving the federal mediation agency and newly convened arbitration boards a steady stream of new cases.
